item.title: Hardware & VRAM Guide for Local Code LLMs
item.description:
You pull a 9B coding model in Ollama, ask it to write a simple function, and your laptop sounds like it’s trying to take flight. Three minutes pass. The fan doesn’t slow down. The output finally arrives — at roughly the pace of someone typing with one finger. You check nvidia-smi. The GPU is maxed out. The model is mostly running on your CPU.

That’s a VRAM problem, and it has a specific, fixable cause.

item.title: Installing and Configuring Ollama for Code Generation
item.description:
You install Ollama, pull a model, and type a prompt into your coding agent. Nothing happens. The cursor blinks. After 45 seconds, the agent returns connection refused. Ollama is running — you can see the icon in the system tray — but the default install was not configured for a coding workflow.

The default Ollama context window is 2,048 tokens (you’ll hit the limit mid-function). The default keep-alive timer unloads the model after 5 minutes of inactivity (a 10–15 second cold-start greets you every time you switch back to it). The API endpoint format your TUI expects differs from Ollama’s native API. None of this is obvious from the install docs.

item.title: Mastering the OpenCode Terminal User Interface
item.description:
Ollama is running. The model loaded. You’ve confirmed it generates clean code from the command line. Now you open a coding session and immediately hit the workflow problem: you type a prompt in one terminal, copy the output, switch to your editor, paste it, check the line numbers, realize they’re wrong, go back to the terminal, correct the prompt, copy again, paste again.

The copy-paste loop is exactly what OpenCode eliminates.

item.title: The Best 7B and 8B Code Models in 2026, and Which Ones Security Will Approve
item.description:
Your head of platform forwards a one-line email from the CISO: “Can we run a code model ourselves instead of sending source code to a vendor?” You already know the shortlist. You’ve read the benchmarks, pulled a couple of models into Ollama on your workstation, and watched one of them write a decent Terraform module in four seconds.

Then you start drafting the answer and realize the benchmarks cover the part nobody on the approval committee will ask about. They’ll ask who trained the model, under what license, where the weights came from, what happens to the code you feed it, and who can reach the server it runs on. “It scored well on HumanEval” doesn’t answer any of those.
